choices: Field injection with @Autowired is required — constructor parameters can't receive beans
Annotate the constructor with @Inject instead — Spring ignores plain constructors
A single constructor is autowired implicitly since Spring 4.3; the failure is elsewhere (e.g., no bean of that type or a circular dependency)
Constructors can't be used for injection at all — switch to setter injection
scenarios.hint: Constructor injection without any annotation has worked for years. If the mechanism is fine, what else makes a dependency unsatisfiable?
scenarios.prompt: Is the missing @Autowired the problem?
scenarios.situation: A service uses constructor injection with no annotations. Startup fails with UnsatisfiedDependencyException and a teammate blames the missing @Autowired.
scenarios.title: The unannotated constructor
scenarios.why: Since Spring 4.3, a single constructor is treated as the autowire candidate without any annotation — constructor injection is the recommended style (final fields, easy testing). The exception means one of the parameter types has no bean definition (missing @Repository/@Component, wrong package scan) or there's a circular reference. Adding @Autowired wouldn't change the outcome.

choices: Move the @Bean method into the @Service class — @Bean only works on service classes
@Bean methods must live in a @Configuration class (or a lite @Component); the @Service class here isn't processed for @Bean definitions the same way
Rename the method to start with 'bean' — Spring only detects that prefix
@Bean requires @Autowired on the method as well
scenarios.hint: Where does Spring documentation say @Bean methods belong — and what does @Configuration add that a plain @Component doesn't?
scenarios.prompt: Why isn't the ObjectMapper bean created?
scenarios.situation: A @Bean method defined inside a @Service class never produces a bean.
scenarios.title: The bean that never existed
scenarios.why: @Bean methods belong in @Configuration classes. A full @Configuration class is subclass-proxied (CGLIB) so inter-bean method calls return the container-managed singleton; in a plain @Component ('lite' mode) the method still registers a bean but calls bypass the container. Putting @Bean inside @Service mixes concerns and, depending on proxying, behaves unexpectedly — the idiomatic home is a dedicated @Configuration class.

choices: Mark both implementations with @Primary — Spring merges them automatically
Delete one implementation — only one bean per interface is allowed
Use @Qualifier("stripeProcessor") at the injection point (or @Primary on the default) to disambiguate which bean to inject
Rename the interface — two implementations of one interface is unsupported
evidence: NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException: expected single matching bean but found 2: stripeProcessor,paypalProcessor
scenarios.hint: The container found two candidates and can't choose. What annotation at the injection point names the winner?
scenarios.prompt: How do you resolve the ambiguity?
scenarios.situation: Two beans implement PaymentProcessor; injecting the interface fails with NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException.
scenarios.title: Two candidates, one injection point
scenarios.why: When multiple beans match a type, Spring needs a tiebreaker: @Qualifier("stripeProcessor") on the injection point selects by bean name, or @Primary on one implementation makes it the default. This is routine in real apps (multiple clients, strategies) — the exception is the container refusing to guess, not a design error.

choices: @Value can only inject from application.properties, not YAML — convert to .properties
The field is static — @Value (and injection generally) doesn't work on static fields; make it an instance field
@Value requires the class to be annotated @ConfigurationProperties as well
Property placeholders need single quotes: @Value('${api.key}')
scenarios.hint: Dependency injection populates instance state on managed beans. What kind of field is `static` — and who owns it?
scenarios.prompt: Why is the injected value always null?
scenarios.situation: An @Value-injected API key is always null at runtime.
scenarios.title: The null API key
scenarios.why: Spring injects values into bean instances; static fields belong to the class, not any instance, so the container never populates them. The fix is an instance field (and constructor or field injection as usual). The same rule applies to @Autowired on statics. If a static accessor is truly needed, set it from a non-static setter — but prefer instance state.

choices: Create a separate @SpringBootApplication class per environment — profiles can't change bean wiring
Define both datasources as beans and annotate the prod one with @Profile("prod") and the dev one with @Profile("dev"), activating via spring.profiles.active
@Profile only works on @Entity classes, not configuration
Profiles are deprecated — use separate Maven modules instead
scenarios.hint: Spring can conditionally register beans based on the active environment name. Which annotation gates a bean on an environment?
scenarios.prompt: How should the two datasources be wired?
scenarios.situation: The app needs H2 in dev and Postgres in prod, selected without code changes.
scenarios.title: One codebase, two databases
scenarios.why: @Profile("dev") / @Profile("prod") on @Bean methods or @Configuration classes registers each datasource only when that profile is active (spring.profiles.active=prod, or application-prod.yml for properties). This keeps environment differences declarative and reviewable. Separate application classes per environment would fork the codebase for a config concern.

choices: The circular dependency must be broken — e.g., extract the shared logic into a third bean, or use setter/lazy injection; constructor cycles can't be satisfied
Add @Lazy to both constructors — that fully resolves all circular dependencies
Circular dependencies are fine in Spring Boot 3; the error must be a typo
Make both beans @Scope("prototype") — prototypes can't have cycles
evidence: BeanCurrentlyInCreationException: Error creating bean 'aService': Requested bean is currently in creation: Is there an unresolvable circular reference?
scenarios.hint: A needs B constructed, B needs A constructed. With constructor injection, which one can possibly be built first?
scenarios.prompt: What is the proper resolution?
scenarios.situation: Two services constructor-inject each other; the context fails to start.
scenarios.title: A needs B needs A
scenarios.why: Constructor injection makes cycles unresolvable by construction: neither bean can be instantiated before the other. (Spring Boot 2.6+ fails fast on cycles instead of silently proxying.) The real fix is structural — extract the shared responsibility into a third bean both depend on. @Lazy or setter injection can paper over it, but a cycle usually signals a design smell worth removing.

choices: Change @PathVariable to @RequestParam — path variables can't be validated
Return null from the handler — Spring converts null to 404 automatically
Return ResponseEntity.notFound().build() when the Optional is empty (or throw a mapped exception) — the handler must decide the status
404 handling is impossible in @RestController; use @Controller instead
scenarios.hint: What HTTP status does a successful-but-empty lookup deserve — and who sets it, the return value or a wrapper?
scenarios.prompt: How should the missing-order case behave?
scenarios.situation: GET /orders/999 returns 200 with an empty body instead of 404.
scenarios.title: The order that wasn't there
scenarios.why: Returning null from a @RestController method produces 200 with an empty body — misleading for clients and caches. ResponseEntity gives full control: return ResponseEntity.of(optional) or map to .notFound().build(). The broader pattern: handlers own their status codes; 404 for absent resources, and a @RestControllerAdvice can centralize it by mapping a custom NotFoundException.

choices: Add @Valid on the @RequestBody parameter and handle MethodArgumentNotValidException (default 400) — or let Spring's default handling return 400
Validation annotations are documentation-only; write manual if-checks in the handler
Return 200 with an error flag in the body — 400 is reserved for malformed JSON
@NotNull only works on @Entity fields, not DTOs
scenarios.hint: The constraints are declared but nothing enforces them. What annotation triggers validation of the request body — and what exception does a violation raise?
scenarios.prompt: How do you turn the annotations into a 400 response?
scenarios.situation: A POST with a null email sails through and blows up deep in the service layer with a 500.
scenarios.title: Validation that never ran
scenarios.why: Jakarta Bean Validation annotations are inert without @Valid (or @Validated) on the @RequestBody parameter. With it, violations raise MethodArgumentNotValidException, which Spring maps to 400 by default — the client learns exactly which fields failed. Manual null checks reimplement the framework; letting it 500 leaks internals and misstates the error.

choices: @GetMapping("/orders/{id}") with @RequestBody — GET requests should carry the payload
@PutMapping("/orders/{id}") replacing the full resource, or @PatchMapping for a partial update — PUT/PATCH are the idempotent update verbs
@PostMapping("/orders/{id}/update") — POST with an action verb in the path is the REST convention
@DeleteMapping followed by @PostMapping — delete then recreate is the atomic update
scenarios.hint: POST is neither safe nor idempotent. Which verbs promise 'repeat this safely' — and what does that buy a client on a flaky network?
scenarios.prompt: What is the idiomatic mapping?
scenarios.situation: An update endpoint uses POST /orders/{id} and works, but a reviewer flags it.
scenarios.title: POST where PUT belongs
scenarios.why: POST is for creating subordinate resources (non-idempotent); full replacement is PUT /orders/{id} (idempotent — safe to retry), partial update is PATCH. Idempotency matters on flaky networks: a retried PUT can't double-apply, while a retried POST might. The mapping is a contract with clients and intermediaries (caches, proxies) that reason about verb semantics.

choices: Catch the exception in every controller method and build the response by hand
Add a @RestControllerAdvice class with @ExceptionHandler methods mapping domain exceptions to status codes and error bodies — one central place
Exceptions in controllers always become 500; the status must be set by a filter
Return ResponseEntity from every method and never throw
evidence:
// today: IllegalArgumentException -> 500 with a stack trace
// want: 400 with {"error": "..."} for bad input, 404 for missing entities
scenarios.hint: You want one place that translates exceptions to HTTP responses for all controllers. Which stereotype does exactly that?
scenarios.prompt: How should this be centralized?
scenarios.situation: Domain exceptions currently escape as 500s with stack traces; the API needs consistent 400/404 error bodies.
scenarios.title: Exceptions escaping as 500s
scenarios.why: @RestControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler methods centralizes the exception-to-response translation: one class maps IllegalArgumentException → 400, EntityNotFoundException → 404, and so on, with a uniform error body. Per-method try/catch duplicates the mapping everywhere; letting stack traces reach clients leaks internals and breaks the API contract.

choices: Add pagination parameters (page, size) via Pageable and return a Page — bounded responses with metadata
Increase the server's max response size — the client can handle it
Return a Stream<Order> and let the client read it incrementally
Compress the JSON — the payload size is the only problem
scenarios.hint: The client asked for 'all orders' and the table has millions of rows. What bounds the response — and what metadata does a client need to page through?
scenarios.prompt: How should the endpoint change?
scenarios.situation: GET /orders returns every row; with 2M orders the service runs out of memory.
scenarios.title: The endpoint that returns everything
scenarios.why: Unbounded list endpoints are a latent outage: data grows until the response OOMs the service or times out. Spring Data's Pageable (page, size, sort) plus a Page<T> return gives bounded queries with total-elements/page-count metadata for clients. Keyset/cursor pagination is the advanced alternative for deep pages; but offset paging via Pageable is the standard first fix.

choices: Content negotiation is automatic for all return types — no configuration needed

Set the produces attribute (or rely on Jackson on the classpath) and return the object — Spring's HttpMessageConverters serialize based on Accept; for CSV add a custom converter or a dedicated endpoint
Return a String of hand-built JSON — converters can't be trusted
Use @ResponseBody on each method — @RestController doesn't include it
scenarios.hint: Who turns the returned object into bytes — and what decides which format wins for a given Accept header?
scenarios.prompt: Why does the JSON endpoint 406 on XML, and how would you add a real CSV format?
scenarios.situation: The JSON report endpoint returns 406 Not Acceptable when a client sends Accept: application/xml.
scenarios.title: The client that wanted XML
scenarios.why: HttpMessageConverters do the serialization: Jackson handles JSON when it's on the classpath, but there's no XML converter without the Jackson XML extension — hence 406 (no converter can produce the accepted type). produces narrows the mapping. For CSV you'd register a custom HttpMessageConverter or a dedicated endpoint; the key insight is that format support is a converter-registration question, not a controller-code question.

choices: Name the method findAllByStatus — Spring Data requires the All infix for filtered queries
findByStatus(String status) — Spring Data derives the query from the method name; no @Query needed for simple predicates
Derived queries only work for findById — write @Query for everything else
Method names can't express queries; use the Criteria API instead
scenarios.hint: Spring Data parses the method name itself. What does `findBy` + a property name generate?
scenarios.prompt: How do you add a find-by-status query?
scenarios.situation: A repository needs a find-by-status query; a teammate starts writing JPQL.
scenarios.title: The query you don't have to write
scenarios.why: Spring Data JPA derives queries from method names: findByStatus(String status) generates select ... where status = ?1 automatically. @Query is for joins, projections, or complex predicates that names can't express. Reaching for JPQL first skips the framework's main convenience — and its compile-time-ish validation of property names.

choices: Call the query twice and merge the results in Java — the database can't join fetch
Add a JOIN FETCH (or @EntityGraph) so items load in the same query — the N+1 comes from lazy loading each collection
Set fetch = FetchType.EAGER on the mapping — eager is always faster
Increase the JDBC fetch size — that batches lazy loads automatically
scenarios.hint: Each `getItems()` triggers a separate SELECT. How do you tell JPA to bring the collection along in the first query?
scenarios.prompt: What causes the N+1, and what is the fix?
scenarios.situation: Loading 200 orders fires 201 queries.
scenarios.title: Two hundred orders, two hundred queries
scenarios.why: @OneToMany collections default to LAZY: the first query loads orders, then each getItems() fires its own SELECT. A JPQL JOIN FETCH (or @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "items")) loads orders with items in one query. EAGER as a global default is the wrong fix — it forces the join on every query including ones that don't need items. Fetch strategy belongs per use-case, not per mapping.

choices: Wrap the multi-step write in a @Transactional service method so all steps commit or roll back together
Call repo.flush() after each step — flush provides atomicity
Catch the exception and manually delete the earlier rows — compensating deletes equal a transaction
Transactions are automatic for any method calling a repository
scenarios.hint: Step 3 throws after steps 1–2 committed. What boundary makes 'all three or none' the unit of work?
scenarios.prompt: How do you make the three steps atomic?
scenarios.situation: placeOrder saves the order, decrements inventory, then the payment charge throws — leaving a persisted order for a failed payment.
scenarios.title: The order that half-happened
scenarios.why: Each repository call runs in its own transaction by default, so step 1 commits before step 3 fails. @Transactional on the service method joins all three steps into one transaction: any RuntimeException rolls everything back. flush() only synchronizes the persistence context — it doesn't define atomicity. Manual compensating deletes are error-prone reimplementations of rollback.

choices: The entity is fine — LazyInitializationException means the database is down
Accessing order.getItems() outside a transaction after the session closed — fetch the collection within the transaction (JOIN FETCH) or map to a DTO inside it
Add @Transactional to the controller — controllers should own transactions
Set spring.jpa.open-in-view=true — it's the recommended fix
scenarios.hint: The service method's transaction ended when it returned. What happens to lazy proxies after their session closes?
scenarios.prompt: Why does the DTO mapping throw?
scenarios.situation: Mapping a lazy collection to a DTO in the controller throws LazyInitializationException.
scenarios.title: The session that closed too early
scenarios.why: Lazy proxies need an open persistence context; the service's transaction (and session) ended at the method return, so touching getItems() in the controller has no session to load from. Fixes: fetch what's needed inside the transaction (JOIN FETCH / entity graph) or do the DTO mapping there. open-in-view keeps the session open through view rendering, but it masks the boundary problem and enables N+1 in templates — fetch deliberately instead.

choices: @GeneratedValue is optional — the database auto-increments by default
@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY) (or a sequence strategy) — without it JPA expects the application to assign the id
Set the id field in the constructor — JPA never generates ids
Use GenerationType.AUTO only — IDENTITY is deprecated
scenarios.hint: `@Id` marks the primary key, but who produces the value? What annotation delegates that to the database?
scenarios.prompt: How should the id be generated?
scenarios.situation: Persisting a new entity fails because no id is assigned.
scenarios.title: The id nobody assigned
scenarios.why: @Id alone declares the primary key; @GeneratedValue says how values are produced. IDENTITY delegates to the database's auto-increment (simple, but batches poorly); SEQUENCE uses a DB sequence (better batching on Postgres/Oracle). Without it, JPA assumes application-assigned ids — correct for natural keys like ISBNs, wrong for surrogate keys.

choices: Use a Pageable query returning Page<Order> and expose page/size/sort params — the database does the slicing
Load all orders and subList in Java — the database is faster at full scans
Cache the full list in a static field and page from memory
Pagination is a frontend concern; the API should return everything
scenarios.hint: Who should do the slicing — the database with LIMIT/OFFSET, or Java after loading 4M rows?
scenarios.prompt: How should the endpoint bound the result?
scenarios.situation: An orders endpoint loads 4M rows into memory.
scenarios.title: Four million rows in a List
scenarios.why: Spring Data's Pageable pushes pagination to the database (LIMIT/OFFSET with a count query), returning Page<T> with total elements and page metadata. Loading everything and slicing in Java just moves the OOM later. For deep pagination, keyset (cursor) paging avoids OFFSET's degrading performance — but Pageable is the standard starting point.

choices: Extend WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter and override configure() — the classic approach
Declare a @Bean SecurityFilterChain using the lambda DSL: http.authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth.requestMatchers("/public/**").permitAll().anyRequest().authenticated())
Security is configured in application.properties only — no Java config needed
Annotate the main class with @EnableWebSecurity and list the paths in its value attribute
evidence:
// TODO: /public/** open, everything else authenticated
// Spring Boot 3 / Spring Security 6
scenarios.hint: WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter was removed in Spring Security 6. What bean now carries the filter-chain configuration?
scenarios.prompt: How is this configured in Spring Security 6?
scenarios.situation: A Spring Boot 3 app needs /public/** open and everything else authenticated.
scenarios.title: Securing the app, the modern way
scenarios.why: Spring Security 6 removed WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter; you now declare a @Bean SecurityFilterChain and configure via the lambda DSL. authorizeHttpRequests replaces the old authorizeRequests, with requestMatchers for path patterns. Ordering matters: specific permitAll rules before anyRequest().authenticated(). Old tutorials showing the adapter class are the #1 source of confusion here.

choices: Store passwords with BCryptPasswordEncoder and verify with matches() — bcrypt is adaptive and salted per password
Use SHA-256 with a single application-wide salt — fast and simple
Encrypt passwords with AES so they can be recovered for the user
Plaintext is fine behind HTTPS — transport security is the protection
scenarios.hint: The encoder bean exists but isn't wired in. Beyond that: what property must the stored value have so a database dump doesn't compromise every account?
scenarios.prompt: How should passwords be stored and verified?
scenarios.situation: A registration flow needs secure password storage; the encoder bean is defined but unused.
scenarios.title: Wiring the password encoder
scenarios.why: BCryptPasswordEncoder hashes with a per-password salt and a configurable work factor — adaptive against faster hardware. passwordEncoder.encode(raw) at registration, matches(raw, stored) at login. Fast hashes (SHA-256) fall to GPU brute force; encryption is reversible (wrong primitive); HTTPS protects transport, not the database at rest.

choices: CSRF protection only matters for browser cookie sessions — stateless JWT APIs typically disable it and rely on the Authorization header
CSRF must stay enabled for all APIs — disabling it is never acceptable
CSRF is handled by the JWT signature — no configuration needed
Move the JWT into a cookie so CSRF protection applies
scenarios.hint: CSRF rides ambient credentials (cookies). Does a Bearer token in the Authorization header get sent automatically by the browser?
scenarios.prompt: Is disabling CSRF here acceptable?
scenarios.situation: A stateless JWT API disables CSRF; a reviewer flags it.
scenarios.title: CSRF on a token API
scenarios.why: CSRF exploits the browser's automatic credential sending — cookies. A JWT in the Authorization header is never sent implicitly, so there's no ambient credential to ride: disabling CSRF for a pure header-token API is standard practice. The flag would be correct if the app used cookie sessions (then keep CSRF enabled). Context decides: match the protection to the credential mechanism.

choices: Check the role manually in each controller method with if-statements
Use @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") on the method with @EnableMethodSecurity — declarative, centralized, testable
Roles can only be enforced in the SecurityFilterChain URL rules — method security doesn't exist
Store the role in a request attribute and check it in a filter
scenarios.hint: URL rules secure paths; what secures the method itself regardless of which URL reaches it?
scenarios.prompt: How should the ADMIN-only rule be enforced?
scenarios.situation: A user-deletion endpoint must be restricted to admins.
scenarios.title: ADMIN only
scenarios.why: @EnableMethodSecurity + @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") enforces authorization at the method level, independent of URL mappings — it survives route refactoring and is unit-testable. Manual if-checks scatter the policy; URL-only rules break when paths change. (Note: hasRole adds the ROLE_ prefix automatically; hasAuthority('ROLE_ADMIN') is the explicit form.)

choices: Permit all access to /actuator/** — monitoring tools need unauthenticated access
Expose only health and info publicly; keep metrics and env behind authentication — env can leak secrets
Disable the actuator entirely — observability is a security risk
Actuator endpoints are secure by default and need no configuration
scenarios.hint: Which of these endpoints can reveal environment variables — and what might those contain?
scenarios.prompt: What is the exposure risk?
scenarios.situation: All actuator endpoints including env are exposed without authentication.
scenarios.title: The actuator that talks too much
scenarios.why: /actuator/env can dump environment variables — often containing secrets — and /actuator/beans, /mappings reveal internals. The safe posture: expose health (and info) for load balancers, keep the rest behind Spring Security rules. management.endpoints.web.exposure.include is an allowlist — treat every entry as a conscious decision.

choices: Validate and sanitize the filename (reject path separators, restrict to an allowlist directory) and serve with content-disposition — the path must never be built from raw user input
Paths from users are safe because Spring sanitizes @PathVariable automatically
Store files in the database instead — the filesystem is inherently insecure
Prefix the user input with the upload directory — concatenation is sufficient
scenarios.hint: What does `name = "../../etc/passwd"` do to that string concatenation?
scenarios.prompt: What is the vulnerability and the fix?
scenarios.situation: A file download endpoint builds a filesystem path from a path variable.
scenarios.title: The download that reads /etc/passwd
scenarios.why: This is path traversal: ../ sequences escape the upload directory and read arbitrary files. Spring does not sanitize path variables for you. The fix: resolve the path, normalize it, and verify it stays under the allowed directory (plus reject separators outright and serve with a safe content-disposition). Concatenation alone is never validation.

choices: @SpringBootTest for everything — slice tests are unreliable
@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class) with MockMvc and @MockBean for the service — tests the web layer in isolation, fast
No test needed — the compiler checks controller mappings
Test with a real running server and RestTemplate only
evidence: // TODO: test POST /orders returns 201 without starting the whole app
scenarios.hint: You want the controller, its mappings, and its filters — but not the database or the full context. Which test slice loads exactly that?
scenarios.prompt: Which test setup fits?
scenarios.situation: A controller test should verify mappings, status codes, and JSON without booting the full application.
scenarios.title: Testing the controller, not the universe
scenarios.why: @WebMvcTest loads only the web layer (controllers, filters, advice) and pairs with MockMvc for request simulation and @MockBean to stub collaborators. It's fast and focused: mapping errors, validation, and serialization are web-layer concerns. @SpringBootTest boots everything — right for integration tests, wasteful for controller unit tests.

choices: Mock the service with @MockBean and verify the controller maps the service result to 201 — the controller's job is HTTP translation, not business logic
Mock the repository inside the controller test — controllers should be tested with real services
Don't mock anything — controller tests must hit the real database
Mock MockMvc itself to avoid HTTP overhead
scenarios.hint: The controller delegates to OrderService. In a web-slice test, what stands in for that collaborator — and what does the test then actually verify?
scenarios.prompt: What should be mocked, and why?
scenarios.situation: A @WebMvcTest fails because the controller's OrderService dependency has no bean in the sliced context.
scenarios.title: The missing bean in the slice
scenarios.why: @WebMvcTest doesn't load @Service beans, so collaborators must be provided as @MockBean (Mockito mocks registered in the sliced context). The test then verifies the controller's responsibility — routing, status codes, request/response mapping — with the service's behavior stubbed. Mocking at the architectural seam keeps the test about the web layer.

choices: @SpringBootTest with the production database — tests should use real infrastructure
@DataJpaTest with an in-memory or Testcontainers database — slices to repositories with a real (or faithful) database
Mock the repository with Mockito — database behavior can be assumed
Repositories are generated code and need no tests
evidence: // TODO: verify findByStatusAndPriority returns the right rows
scenarios.hint: You need to verify actual query semantics — derived names, @Query JPQL, mappings. What can execute those without booting the whole app?
scenarios.prompt: How should the custom query be tested?
scenarios.situation: A derived query method needs verification against real database semantics.
scenarios.title: Testing the query, not the mock
scenarios.why: @DataJpaTest slices the context to JPA components (repositories, entities) with a test database — in-memory by default, or Testcontainers for production fidelity (Postgres-specific SQL won't run on H2). Mocking the repository would test the mock, not the query. Query logic is exactly the kind of thing that must run against a real database.

choices: H2 is identical to Postgres — no changes needed
Skip database tests in CI — they're too slow to matter
Use Testcontainers to run the real Postgres in Docker for integration tests — H2 can't validate Postgres-specific SQL
Rewrite all queries in H2 dialect and translate at deploy time
evidence:
@Query(value = "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE data @> :filter", nativeQuery = true)

Testcontainers starts a real Postgres in Docker for the test run, giving true fidelity. @DataJpaTest + Testcontainers is the standard combo: sliced context, production-identical database. The cost is Docker in CI, which is table stakes for backend testing.

choices: Assert that service.create() was called — verifying the mock proves the wiring
Stub the service to return a saved order, perform the POST, and assert 201 plus the JSON body — verify the HTTP contract

scenarios.hint: The controller's contract with the outside world is HTTP: status, headers, body. Which assertions test that contract?

scenarios.situation: A MockMvc test exists but only verifies a mock interaction; it wouldn't catch a broken status code or malformed JSON.
scenarios.title: Testing the mock instead of the API
scenarios.why: In a web-slice test, the valuable assertions are on the HTTP contract: mvc.perform(post("/orders")...) → andExpect(status().isCreated()), jsonPath("$.id").exists(), content().contentType(...). Verifying the mock was called tests the test's own setup. The controller's job is translation between HTTP and the service — assert the translation.

choices: Run the full @SpringBootTest suite on every commit — comprehensive beats fast
Keep a fast unit/slice suite for every commit and run the heavy integration suite on a schedule or pre-merge — tier the feedback by cost

evidence: # CI: 45-minute @SpringBootTest suite on every push; developers stop waiting for it

scenarios.situation: A 45-minute full-context suite runs on every push; developers merge without waiting.

lessons.title: Core & DI — Core concepts
concepts: Dependency injection: when multiple beans match a type, Spring needs a tiebreaker: @Qualifier("stripeProcessor") on the injection point selects by bean name, or @Primary on one implementation makes it the default.
Constructor injection makes cycles unresolvable by construction: neither bean can be instantiated before the other. Fix it by an instance field (and constructor or field injection as usual).

@Configuration: @Bean methods belong in @Configuration classes. @Profile("dev") / @Profile("prod") on @Bean methods or @Configuration classes registers each datasource only when that profile is active (spring.profiles.active=prod, or application-prod.yml for properties).

@Bean: putting @Bean inside @Service mixes concerns and, depending on proxying, behaves unexpectedly — the idiomatic home is a dedicated @Configuration class. Spring injects values into bean instances; static fields belong to the class, not any instance, so the container never populates them.

example.walkthrough: @Profile("dev") / @Profile("prod") on @Bean methods or @Configuration classes registers each datasource only when that profile is active (spring.profiles.active=prod, or application-prod.yml for properties). This keeps environment differences declarative and reviewable. Separate application classes per environment would fork the codebase for a config concern.

pitfalls: Common trap: a single constructor is autowired implicitly since Spring 4.3; the failure is elsewhere (e.g., no bean of that type or a circular dependency).
Common trap: @Bean methods must live in a @Configuration class (or a lite @Component); the @Service class here isn't processed for @Bean definitions the same way.
Common trap: circular dependencies are fine in Spring Boot 3; the error must be a typo.
Common trap: property placeholders need single quotes: @Value('${api.key}').

lessons.title: Web & REST — Core concepts
concepts: ResponseEntity gives full control: return ResponseEntity.of(optional) or map to .notFound().build().
Status codes: the broader pattern: handlers own their status codes; 404 for absent resources, and a @RestControllerAdvice can centralize it by mapping a custom NotFoundException.
Bean Validation: jakarta Bean Validation annotations are inert without @Valid (or @Validated) on the @RequestBody parameter.

example.walkthrough: Jakarta Bean Validation annotations are inert without @Valid (or @Validated) on the @RequestBody parameter. With it, violations raise MethodArgumentNotValidException, which Spring maps to 400 by default — the client learns exactly which fields failed. Manual null checks reimplement the framework; letting it 500 leaks internals and misstates the error.

pitfalls: Common trap: content negotiation is automatic for all return types.
Common trap: return ResponseEntity.notFound().build() when the Optional is empty (or throw a mapped exception).
Common trap: catch the exception in every controller method and build the response by hand.
Common trap: validation annotations are documentation-only; write manual if-checks in the handler.

lessons.title: Data & JPA — Core concepts
concepts: Derived queries: spring Data JPA derives queries from method names: findByStatus(String status) generates select ... where status = ?1 automatically. @Query is for joins, projections, or complex predicates that names can't express.

N+1: fixes: fetch what's needed inside the transaction (JOIN FETCH / entity graph) or do the DTO mapping there. open-in-view keeps the session open through view rendering, but it masks the boundary problem and enables N+1 in templates — fetch deliberately instead.
JOIN FETCH: a JPQL JOIN FETCH (or @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "items")) loads orders with items in one query.

@Transactional: each repository call runs in its own transaction by default, so step 1 commits before step 3 fails. @Transactional on the service method joins all three steps into one transaction: any RuntimeException rolls everything back. flush() only synchronizes the persistence context — it doesn't define atomicity.

example.walkthrough: Spring Data JPA derives queries from method names: findByStatus(String status) generates select ... where status = ?1 automatically. @Query is for joins, projections, or complex predicates that names can't express. Reaching for JPQL first skips the framework's main convenience — and its compile-time-ish validation of property names.

pitfalls: Common trap: spring Data requires the All infix for filtered queries.
Common trap: derived queries only work for findById.
Common trap: method names can't express queries; use the Criteria API instead.
Common trap: accessing order.getItems() outside a transaction after the session closed.

lessons.title: Security — Core concepts
concepts: SecurityFilterChain: spring Security 6 removed WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter; you now declare a @Bean SecurityFilterChain and configure via the lambda DSL. authorizeHttpRequests replaces the old authorizeRequests, with requestMatchers for path patterns.

Authorization rules: @EnableMethodSecurity + @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") enforces authorization at the method level, independent of URL mappings — it survives route refactoring and is unit-testable.

PasswordEncoder: bCryptPasswordEncoder hashes with a per-password salt and a configurable work factor — adaptive against faster hardware. passwordEncoder.encode(raw) at registration, matches(raw, stored) at login.
CSRF exploits the browser's automatic credential sending — cookies.

example.code:
// TODO: /public/** open, everything else authenticated
// Spring Boot 3 / Spring Security 6
example.walkthrough: Spring Security 6 removed WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter; you now declare a @Bean SecurityFilterChain and configure via the lambda DSL. authorizeHttpRequests replaces the old authorizeRequests, with requestMatchers for path patterns. Ordering matters: specific permitAll rules before anyRequest().authenticated(). Old tutorials showing the adapter class are the #1 source of confusion here.

pitfalls: Common trap: use @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") on the method with @EnableMethodSecurity.
Common trap: CSRF protection only matters for browser cookie sessions.
Common trap: move the JWT into a cookie so CSRF protection applies.
Common trap: check the role manually in each controller method with if-statements.

lessons.title: Testing — Core concepts
concepts: MockMvc: @WebMvcTest loads only the web layer (controllers, filters, advice) and pairs with MockMvc for request simulation and @MockBean to stub collaborators.
@WebMvcTest doesn't load @Service beans, so collaborators must be provided as @MockBean (Mockito mocks registered in the sliced context).

Test doubles: @DataJpaTest slices the context to JPA components (repositories, entities) with a test database — in-memory by default, or Testcontainers for production fidelity (Postgres-specific SQL won't run on H2).
Repository tests: mocking the repository would test the mock, not the query. Verifying the mock was called tests the test's own setup.

example.code:

lessons.title: Spring Boot — Core concepts
concepts: Inversion of control means the framework wires your objects: declare dependencies via constructor injection, keep fields final, and your classes become both Spring-managed and plain-unit-testable.

Controllers translate HTTP into method calls and back. Keep them thin — validation and status mapping at the edge (@Valid, @ControllerAdvice) — and push business rules into @Service beans with clear transaction boundaries.

JPA associations are lazy by default for a reason. Fetch explicitly what each use case needs (fetch joins, @EntityGraph, DTO projections) inside the service's transaction; never let the JSON serializer drive your queries.
@Transactional manages the database transaction, nothing else. External side effects (payments, emails, messages) need compensation logic — a rollback cannot unsend an email.

Spring Security is a filter chain: authentication filters establish identity, authorization rules decide access. Public endpoints must bypass auth filters, and sensitive infrastructure (like Actuator) gets its own locked-down exposure.
Actuator and metrics are production features, not debug conveniences. Expose health/info to the platform, secure everything else, and alert on what the metrics tell you before users do.

example.walkthrough: Constructor injection keeps the controller testable; @Valid triggers bean validation before business logic; @ResponseStatus(CREATED) returns the correct 201. The @ControllerAdvice turns unparseable JSON into a clean 400 instead of a confusing default.

pitfalls: Common trap: field injection with @Autowired — works at runtime, breaks plain unit tests, and hides required dependencies; prefer constructor injection.
Common trap: @Transactional on the controller or relying on Open-Session-in-View — lazy proxies get serialized into N+1 queries and LazyInitializationExceptions.
Common trap: exposing all Actuator endpoints — env and heapdump leak secrets; expose health/info only, secure the rest.
Common trap: assuming @Transactional rolls back external calls — it only rolls back the database; design compensating actions for real-world side effects.

simulations.title: The 404 that wasn't
simulations.brief: GET /hello returns 404, but HelloController exists and the app starts cleanly. The endpoint is 'right there' — except it isn't.

steps.symptom: GET /hello → 404. The application starts with no errors.
options: Read the controller: hello() has no mapping annotation, so Spring exposes no route for it
The controller is in the wrong module
steps.explain: A @RestController method without @GetMapping (or similar) is never registered — no mapping, no route, 404.

evidence: Mapped "{[/error]}" onto handler — no mapping for /hello
options: Add @RequestMapping at the class level only
Move the method to another controller
Change the return type to ResponseEntity
steps.explain: The method needs its own mapping: @GetMapping("/hello") registers the route with the DispatcherServlet.

steps.symptom: Fix applied. Verify the route is live.
options: Confirm the startup log shows the GET /hello mapping and curl it for a 200
Confirm the annotation is spelled correctly
steps.explain: The startup mapping log is the proof of registration; a 200 from the endpoint is the proof of behavior.

simulations.debrief: Spring 404s are usually missing mappings, not missing code. Read the controller for the annotation, add it, and verify via the startup mapping log.

simulations.title: Request lifecycle
simulations.brief: Restore the order a request travels through a Spring Boot web application.

steps.context: Arrange the request lifecycle stages in execution order.
items: Servlet filter chain (security, logging)
DispatcherServlet receives the request
HandlerMapping finds the controller method
Controller executes and returns a value
HttpMessageConverter serializes the response

simulations.debrief: Filters → DispatcherServlet → HandlerMapping → controller → message converter. Knowing the chain tells you exactly where to look when a stage misbehaves.

simulations.title: 401 or 403?
simulations.brief: Two users hit /admin and get different statuses. Triage like a security engineer.

steps.text: User A (no credentials sent) gets 401 Unauthorized on /admin. Correct reading?

choices.label: 401 means unauthenticated — no (or bad) credentials were presented; the fix is to authenticate
Retry with the same request
choices.feedback: Retrying without credentials returns the same 401.

steps.text: User B (valid login, role USER) gets 403 Forbidden on /admin. Correct reading and fix?

choices.label: 403 means authenticated but not authorized — grant the ADMIN role or adjust the access rule
choices.feedback: Right: 403 = 'I know who you are, and the answer is no.' Fix the authorization, not the login.

choices.label: Tell user B to log in again
choices.feedback: Re-authenticating won't change authorization — the login already succeeded.

choices.label: Disable security for /admin
choices.feedback: Disabling security 'fixes' the symptom by removing the protection.

simulations.debrief: 401 = unauthenticated (prove who you are); 403 = unauthorized (you're known, but not allowed). Never confuse the two when triaging.

consoleSims.title: Fix the missing mapping
consoleSims.brief: HelloController.hello() has no mapping annotation and /hello returns 404. Add the annotation in the IDE.

tasks.instruction: Open HelloController.java in the code editor.
tasks.hint: Find HelloController.java in the file explorer.

tasks.instruction: Add @GetMapping("/hello") on the line above the hello() method.
tasks.hint: Mapping annotations go directly above the handler method.

tasks.instruction: Restart the app in the IDE and confirm /hello returns 200.
tasks.hint: Use the Run control, then check the endpoint.

sections.heading: Core & DI
items: Dependency injection — when multiple beans match a type, Spring needs a tiebreaker: @Qualifier("stripeProcessor") on the injection point selects by bean name, or @Primary on one implementation makes it the default.
Constructor injection makes cycles unresolvable by construction — neither bean can be instantiated before the other. Fix it by an instance field (and constructor or field injection as usual).
Common trap — a single constructor is autowired implicitly since Spring 4.3; the failure is elsewhere (e.g., no bean of that type or a circular dependency).
Common trap — @Bean methods must live in a @Configuration class (or a lite @Component); the @Service class here isn't processed for @Bean definitions the same way.
Common trap — circular dependencies are fine in Spring Boot 3; the error must be a typo.
Common trap — property placeholders need single quotes: @Value('${api.key}').

sections.heading: Web & REST
items: ResponseEntity gives full control — return ResponseEntity.of(optional) or map to .notFound().build().
Status codes — the broader pattern: handlers own their status codes; 404 for absent resources, and a @RestControllerAdvice can centralize it by mapping a custom NotFoundException.
Bean Validation — jakarta Bean Validation annotations are inert without @Valid (or @Validated) on the @RequestBody parameter.
Common trap — content negotiation is automatic for all return types.
Common trap — return ResponseEntity.notFound().build() when the Optional is empty (or throw a mapped exception).
Common trap — catch the exception in every controller method and build the response by hand.
Common trap — validation annotations are documentation-only; write manual if-checks in the handler.

items: Derived queries — spring Data JPA derives queries from method names: findByStatus(String status) generates select ... where status = ?1 automatically. @Query is for joins, projections, or complex predicates that names can't express.

sections.heading: Security
items: SecurityFilterChain — spring Security 6 removed WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter; you now declare a @Bean SecurityFilterChain and configure via the lambda DSL. authorizeHttpRequests replaces the old authorizeRequests, with requestMatchers for path patterns.

Authorization rules — @EnableMethodSecurity + @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") enforces authorization at the method level, independent of URL mappings — it survives route refactoring and is unit-testable.

PasswordEncoder — bCryptPasswordEncoder hashes with a per-password salt and a configurable work factor — adaptive against faster hardware. passwordEncoder.encode(raw) at registration, matches(raw, stored) at login.
CSRF exploits the browser's automatic credential sending — cookies.
Common trap — use @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") on the method with @EnableMethodSecurity.
Common trap — CSRF protection only matters for browser cookie sessions.
Common trap — move the JWT into a cookie so CSRF protection applies.
Common trap — check the role manually in each controller method with if-statements.

sections.heading: Testing
items: MockMvc — @WebMvcTest loads only the web layer (controllers, filters, advice) and pairs with MockMvc for request simulation and @MockBean to stub collaborators.

Test doubles — @DataJpaTest slices the context to JPA components (repositories, entities) with a test database — in-memory by default, or Testcontainers for production fidelity (Postgres-specific SQL won't run on H2).
Repository tests — mocking the repository would test the mock, not the query. Verifying the mock was called tests the test's own setup.
Common trap — controller tests must hit the real database.
Common trap — mock the repository inside the controller test.
Common trap — mock MockMvc itself to avoid HTTP overhead.
Common trap — test with a real running server and RestTemplate only.

Externalized configuration — server.port in application.properties (or SERVER_PORT env var, which takes precedence) changes the port with zero code changes — that's the point of externalized configuration.
Executable jars — (Layered jars via layers.idx go further, optimizing Docker layer caching — same plugin, more config.).
Common trap — executable jars are impossible; deploy a WAR to Tomcat instead.
Common trap — health checks are unnecessary with Spring Boot.

The repackage goal restructures the jar — your classes under BOOT-INF/classes, dependencies under BOOT-INF/lib, and Spring Boot's JarLauncher as the manifest Main-Class. Without it you have a plain library jar.

checklist: Get 7–8 hours of sleep the night before — fatigue destroys recall faster than any topic gap.
Bring valid government-issued photo ID and arrive at the test center 30 minutes early.
Eat a real meal beforehand; bring water and a light snack if the center allows them.
Read every question twice before scanning the answer choices.
Flag uncertain questions and move on — return with fresh eyes at the end.
Eliminate the obviously wrong answers first, then compare the survivors.
Budget your time: answer steadily and keep a 10–15 minute review buffer.
Re-run your weakest-domain drill until mastery is at least 80%.
For Core & DI: restate the 'why' behind each scenario answer in your own words — if you can't explain it, you don't own it.
Redo one Web & REST lab from scratch without looking at the steps.
Recite the key Data & JPA terms from the glossary aloud from memory.
